Local Tastes
Ropa vieja
Cuba's national dish — slow-braised flank steak shredded into long fibres and stewed with tomato, peppers, onion, and cumin until deeply flavoured. Served at virtually every paladar and most hotel restaurants.
El Rum Rum de La Habana and paladares across Old Havana
Moros y Cristianos
Black beans cooked with white rice — "Moors and Christians" — the standard Cuban side dish, eaten with nearly every meal and made more complex by some cooks with sofrito, bay leaf, and a splash of Cuban wine.
Served with nearly every meal at paladares across Havana
Tostones
Green plantains sliced, smashed flat, and twice-fried until golden and crisp — the Cuban version of potato crisps, eaten salted as a snack or alongside grilled fish and pork at paladares all over Havana.
Available at paladares and street stalls throughout the city
Mojito
White rum, fresh lime, raw sugar, mint, and soda — Havana's signature cocktail, associated with La Bodeguita del Medio where Hemingway drank them. The quality varies sharply; order at a seated bar, never from a street cart.
La Bodeguita del Medio · Calle Empedrado 207 · Habana Vieja
Daiquiri
Havana Club rum blended with lime juice and sugar — Hemingway's version adds grapefruit juice and maraschino liqueur and was invented at El Floridita on Calle Obispo, steps from the hotel.
El Floridita · Calle Obispo 557 · Habana Vieja
Café cubano
An espresso-strength dark roast brewed in a Moka pot with raw sugar dissolved directly in the grounds — served in a thimble-sized cup, intensely sweet, and the daily fuel of Havana from early morning until late afternoon.
El Café · Calle Amargura 358 · Habana Vieja
Food Delivery
No mainstream delivery apps operate in Havana — Uber Eats, Bolt Food, and similar services do not cover Cuba. Paladares take phone or in-person orders; ask your hotel concierge for nearby options.

Getting Around
No ride-hailing apps operate in Havana — Uber, Bolt, and similar services do not cover Cuba. State taxis — yellow metered Cubataxi cabs — are the most reliable option for tourists; agree on the fare before you ride or ensure the meter is running. Bicitaxis are plentiful in Old Havana for short hops. Private taxi drivers negotiated at your hotel are the practical choice for the Viñales day trip.
Worth Knowing

Bring cash — US cards don't work anywhere in Cuba

US-issued credit and debit cards are blocked across Cuba — this includes Visa and Mastercard from US banks, Apple Pay, and Google Pay linked to US accounts. Bring sufficient EUR, Canadian dollars, or British pounds; CADECA exchange offices and bank branches convert these at the best rate. The USD attracts a 10% exchange surcharge, so avoid it if possible.

Cuba's sole legal currency is the Cuban Peso — CUP. The old tourist peso, CUC, has been abolished. Tourist-facing prices at international hotels are often quoted in USD and then converted at the desk; street vendors, paladares, and taxis quote in CUP. ATMs at major hotels are frequently out of cash — carry a cash reserve before each day out.

Cuba's internet infrastructure is state-run and slow. Wi-fi is available at hotel lobbies, Etecsa hotspots in public plazas, and some paladares — buy a NAUTA card at an Etecsa office to connect. Your hotel room may have reliable wi-fi; check at check-in. Roaming from a foreign SIM is unreliable.

Photographing military installations, police officers, and government buildings is prohibited. Some Cubans will ask for a small payment to be photographed — ask before pointing a camera at anyone. Old Havana's streets, plazas, and classic cars are entirely open to photography.

The US State Department rates Cuba at Level 2 — Exercise Increased Caution — primarily for petty theft, scams targeting tourists, and occasional civil unrest. Old Havana is generally safe to walk at night, but keep valuables out of sight and be cautious in quieter Centro Habana streets after dark.
